question.problem:
The substitution $z={y}^{-2}$ can be used to transform the equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}y(1-x{y}^{2})
$$

into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)+P(x)z(x)=Q(x).$ What is the function $Q(x)?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{-2}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-2{y}^{-3}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{2}{z}^{-3/2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}{z}^{-3/2}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{z}^{-1/2}(1-x{z}^{-1}) \\ {z}^{-3/2}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & ={x}^{2}{z}^{-1/2}(x{z}^{-1}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

We now write the above equation in standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x).
$$

In doing so, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & ={x}^{2}z(x{z}^{-1}-1) \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & ={x}^{3}-{x}^{2}z \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+{x}^{2}z & ={x}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $Q(x)={x}^{3}.$
